This paper studies a simple but important mismatch in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful proof trajectories, yet at inference time they operate inside a search process that repeatedly proposes tactics, observes failures, and backtracks. The paper proposes to expose the model to trial-and-error traces during fine-tuning, and to let the model explicitly emit backtracking instructions at inference time. To support this study, the authors construct PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset of intuitionistic propositional logic theorems paired with proof-search traces generated by a focused proof search procedure. Empirically, the proposed TrialMaster model appears to outperform a conventional LLM-guided DFS baseline on an out-of-distribution split defined by proof length, while also reducing the number of Lean calls.

I found the core intuition compelling. The train-test discrepancy identified in the introduction is real and underexplored: theorem provers do not merely need to imitate successful next steps, they need to behave sensibly after unsuccessful exploration. The paper also has a nice systems flavor in that it does not just add negative examples to training, but changes the inference interface so that the model can condition on prior failed branches and can explicitly decide to backtrack. The creation of a Lean-checked dataset with proof-search traces is also potentially valuable, especially because open theorem-proving datasets rarely expose full search trees.

That said, while the paper is interesting and promising, I have substantial concerns about the strength of the empirical claims, the fairness of the comparisons, and the extent to which the conclusions generalize beyond this synthetic setting. In its current form, I would view the paper as a useful exploratory study rather than a definitive demonstration.

The main strength is the clarity of the problem formulation. The paper isolates a concrete hypothesis: learning from failed proof attempts should improve tactic generation and search efficiency. The experimental setup is also reasonably controlled in one important sense: the domain is restricted to intuitionistic propositional logic, proofs are machine-checkable in Lean, and the data generation process is algorithmic. This makes it possible to study the effect of trial-and-error supervision without many confounds from noisy human-written proofs or large libraries. The ablation in Table 3 is especially important: using the same inference style but removing trial-and-error from training causes a large drop in OOD success rate, which supports the central claim better than the comparison to DFS alone.

However, the paper’s headline comparison between TrialMaster and the “conventional DFS system” is not fully apples-to-apples. TrialMaster and DFS differ along multiple axes simultaneously: training data, inference procedure, decoding strategy, and failure handling. TrialMaster uses greedy one-step generation conditioned on the entire proof-search history and can emit explicit backtrack instructions that do not incur Lean calls. The DFS baseline samples multiple tactics per state with varying temperature, explores them externally, and is subject to a hard step budget. This means the observed gains cannot be attributed cleanly to “learning from failure” alone. Some of the advantage may come from the richer inference interface, some from the serialization of search history into the prompt, some from the fact that backtracking instructions are free under the chosen cost metric, and some from the training data. The ablation in Table 3 partially addresses this, but only for one alternative baseline. The paper would be much stronger if it systematically disentangled these factors.

Relatedly, the search-cost metric favors TrialMaster in a somewhat structural way. The paper counts only Lean calls, and explicitly notes that backtracking instructions do not require Lean and therefore do not add cost. But TrialMaster may still consume substantial model inference budget by repeatedly generating long outputs conditioned on an ever-growing proof tree. Since the method prompts with “all history paths” and asks the model to output the entire proof path each time, its actual computational cost may be dominated by LLM decoding rather than Lean calls. By contrast, the DFS baseline makes one inference per state and then spends cost in Lean. If the claim is efficiency, the paper should report wall-clock time, number of model tokens generated, number of model forward passes, or at least a combined cost metric. As written, “lower search cost” really means “fewer Lean checks,” which is narrower than the wording suggests.

I also have concerns about the dataset claims, especially the repeated use of “complete, scalable, and representative.” The theorem generation procedure may indeed define a bijection between natural numbers and formulas under a grammar and ordering, but representativeness of formulas does not imply representativeness of provable theorems, nor of proof-search phenomena encountered in broader theorem proving. The dataset is restricted to intuitionistic propositional logic with a fixed number of internal nodes and a bounded number of atoms, and proofs are generated by a specific focused proof search algorithm with a particular polarization scheme and an additional incompleteness-inducing heuristic. This is a very specific synthetic distribution. It is useful, but the paper overstates what can be concluded from it. In particular, the proof traces reflect the behavior of the FPS generator, so TrialMaster may be learning to imitate that search policy, including its backtracking style, rather than learning a broadly useful notion of “failure-aware reasoning.”

The incompleteness introduced in proof generation deserves more scrutiny than it receives. The paper states that once an implication is picked, it cannot be used to show its premise, and that this only affects about 1 in 1000 randomly sampled provable theorems. This may sound negligible, but it means the dataset and evaluation are tied to a search procedure that is not fully complete. Since the model is trained and tested on traces from this procedure, it is unclear whether success means proving the theorem in general or reproducing proofs accessible under this restricted search regime. At minimum, the paper should quantify how many sampled formulas are provable in intuitionistic logic but excluded by the heuristic, and whether any test instances are impacted.

The OOD split is sensible in spirit but not entirely convincing as evidence of generalization. The split is based on proof length quantiles, with training below the 0.66 quantile and OOD above the 0.8 quantile, while theorem statements all have 16 internal nodes. This creates a harder split, but it is still within the same synthetic formula distribution and same proof generator. It would be helpful to know whether the OOD set differs in theorem structure, connective composition, branching factor, or proof-tree depth, not just token length. More importantly, because the proofs with trial-and-error are generated by random choices during chaining and the training set uses two of the shortest five traces, the model may be benefiting from a curriculum toward cleaner traces rather than from failure information per se. Table 4 suggests longer traces hurt, which is interesting, but it also raises the possibility that the gains come from a carefully curated subset of traces rather than from the general principle of learning from failure.

The inference protocol for TrialMaster is also somewhat unusual and under-specified. The model is prompted with the entire proof-search history and asked to output the “entire proof path after,” but only the first tactic is used. This is a peculiar decoding setup: the model is trained or prompted to continue a long structured trace, yet evaluation only consumes the first action. It would be useful to know whether directly training a next-action predictor over the same history performs similarly. If so, the current formulation may be unnecessarily expensive. If not, that would itself be an interesting result. Similarly, the paper says that any Lean error immediately terminates TrialMaster’s search attempt, whereas DFS can continue exploring alternatives after invalid tactics at a state. This asymmetry may either hurt or help TrialMaster depending on the regime, but it should be discussed more explicitly.

The empirical presentation is weaker than it should be for a paper making comparative claims. Several key numerical results are only described qualitatively because Figure 5 is referenced but not fully available in the text provided. The paper should include complete tables for OOD success rate and cost across all hyperparameter settings, not just plots and selected highlights. Confidence intervals or multiple random seeds are also missing. Given that proof generation involves randomization and model fine-tuning can vary materially across runs, reporting single numbers without variance makes it hard to assess robustness. This is especially important because some claimed differences are small, e.g., 0.3% success-rate gaps paired with large cost differences.

I also think the baseline set is too narrow. Comparing against one LLM-guided DFS baseline is a start, but the paper itself cites work such as Baldur and COPRA that incorporate richer feedback or backtracking-related information. Even if those systems are not directly portable to this domain, the paper could include stronger internal baselines: for example, a DFS system whose prompt includes failed tactics and prior states but whose model is trained only on successful proofs; a model trained with trial-and-error traces but used inside DFS rather than self-backtracking; or a model trained with explicit negative examples but without backtrack tokens. These would help isolate whether the key benefit comes from negative supervision, from explicit backtrack-action modeling, or from conditioning on search history.

Another issue is that the paper’s claim that the model “learns backtracking capability” is currently supported only by format correctness: all backtracking instructions point to existing state numbers and follow the correct format. That is not enough. The important question is whether the backtracking decisions are semantically useful: do they return to states from which successful continuation is likely, do they avoid repeated failures, and how often do they improve over naive policies? A stronger analysis would report the frequency of backtrack actions, the proportion that lead to eventual proof completion, and comparisons to simple heuristics such as always backtracking one level or using external DFS over the same one-step model.

There are also some presentation and rigor issues. The paper occasionally overclaims from limited evidence, and some methodological details are missing or ambiguous. For example, the exact prompt format, serialization of states, and training targets are not described in enough detail for reproducibility. It is unclear how many tokens the average training example contains, how often the 1500-word limit is hit for each method, and whether “word length” corresponds to tokenizer length or whitespace-separated words. Since context limits are central to the method, this matters. The training setup is also minimalistic—single epoch, batch size 4, one backbone model—and it is not clear whether the conclusions are stable across model sizes or training budgets.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has merit. The synthetic setting is not a flaw by itself; in fact, it is a reasonable place to test the hypothesis cleanly. The dataset could be useful to the community, and the central idea of exposing theorem-proving models to failed search trajectories is plausible and likely relevant beyond propositional logic. The paper’s strongest evidence is the within-method ablation showing a large gain from trial-and-error training under the same inference style. If the authors sharpen the claims and strengthen the experimental controls, this could become a solid contribution.

I would encourage the authors to revise along the following lines. First, make the causal story cleaner with stronger ablations: same inference, different training; same training, different inference; explicit backtrack token versus no backtrack token; conditioning on failed history versus not. Second, report fuller OOD results in tables, with variance across seeds and additional efficiency metrics beyond Lean calls. Third, analyze the backtracking behavior itself rather than only its syntactic validity. Fourth, moderate the claims about representativeness and generality, and discuss more candidly that the model is trained on traces from a specific proof-search algorithm in a restricted logic. Fifth, clarify the exact data format, prompt structure, and token-length statistics to improve reproducibility.

In summary, I find the paper interesting and directionally valuable, with a good motivating idea and a potentially useful dataset. But the current empirical evidence does not yet fully support the broader claims, mainly because the main comparison conflates several factors and the evaluation is confined to a narrow synthetic domain. My overall assessment is moderately positive on novelty and intuition, but cautious on rigor and generality. If accepted, it would be as an exploratory contribution that opens an important question rather than as a definitive answer.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper studies whether large language models for theorem proving benefit from training on trial-and-error trajectories rather than only successful proof paths. The authors introduce PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset of intuitionistic propositional logic theorems with proofs generated by a focused proof search procedure, including backtracking traces. They fine-tune Llama-2-7B in two settings: (1) TrialMaster, trained on proofs with trial-and-error information and performing greedy sequential inference with explicit backtrack instructions, and (2) a conventional DFS-based prover trained only on correct proof paths and using sampled tactics during search. On a split designed to separate shorter-proof training examples from longer-proof OOD test examples, TrialMaster reportedly achieves higher OOD success rate and lower Lean-call search cost than the DFS baseline, and substantially outperforms an ablation that uses the same inference style but is trained without trial-and-error data.
strengths: The paper addresses a real mismatch in neural theorem proving between training on only successful trajectories and inference-time exploration over many failed attempts.
The proposed idea is intuitive and practically relevant: exposing the model to failed branches and backtracking history may improve tactic quality and search efficiency.
The authors build a new Lean-checked dataset with explicit trial-and-error traces, which is potentially useful for future work.
The experimental setup includes both success rate and search-cost measurements, which is appropriate for theorem proving systems.
The ablation comparing the same inference style with and without trial-and-error training provides evidence that the gains are not solely due to the inference protocol.
The paper is clearly motivated and the overall methodology is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow: all experiments are on synthetic intuitionistic propositional logic theorems generated by a deterministic proof-search procedure, so it is unclear how much the conclusions transfer to realistic theorem proving domains.
The main comparison is not fully controlled because TrialMaster and the DFS baseline differ in both training data and inference/search procedure, making causal attribution difficult.

The claim that PropL is 'uniformly sampled from all possible theorems' or 'representative of all intuitionistic propositional logic theorems' is overstated and insufficiently justified, especially given the fixed formula size and theorem filtering.
The proof generator includes an explicitly incomplete heuristic ('once an implication is picked, the implication cannot be used to show its premise'), which may bias the dataset and learned behavior.
The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple random-seed runs are reported despite stochastic proof generation and model fine-tuning.

The paper does not compare against stronger or more relevant baselines such as training on failed attempts without explicit backtrack tokens, using error messages, or prompting/search methods that also condition on prior failures.
The context/window and stopping criteria differ in ways that may advantage one method or complicate interpretation of search-cost comparisons.
The dataset construction and theorem/proof distributions are not characterized in enough detail to assess diversity, difficulty, or possible train-test leakage through structural similarity.
methodological_flaws: The central experimental claim conflates two factors: TrialMaster differs from the DFS baseline in both supervision signal and inference algorithm. Therefore, the headline improvement over DFS does not isolate the effect of learning from failure. The ablation helps, but it does not replace a fully matched comparison against a model trained with trial-and-error but decoded under DFS, or vice versa.

The paper's representativeness argument is scientifically weak. A bijection from natural numbers to formulas does not by itself imply a meaningful uniform distribution over the space of theorems encountered in practice, and fixing the number of internal nodes to 16 further narrows the distribution. Moreover, only provable/generated instances with available proofs are effectively used, which changes the induced distribution.

The proof-generation process is not a neutral source of supervision: all proofs and failed branches come from the same FPS algorithm. As a result, the model may primarily learn to imitate the idiosyncratic search behavior of that algorithm rather than acquire generally useful failure-aware reasoning.

The additional incompleteness assumption in proof search introduces a systematic bias into the dataset. Even if it affects only about 1 in 1000 sampled provable theorems, this claim is not substantiated with a formal analysis, and it undermines the 'complete' characterization of the dataset/search traces.

Search-cost comparisons are not entirely apples-to-apples. TrialMaster emits backtrack instructions that incur no Lean calls, while DFS must validate sampled tactics through Lean. Since the systems expose different action spaces and verification pathways, lower Lean-call counts do not purely reflect better theorem-proving efficiency.

Failure conditions are asymmetric and may distort success-rate comparisons. TrialMaster fails immediately on any Lean error, whereas DFS can continue exploring alternative sampled tactics after invalid suggestions at a state. Conversely, TrialMaster's history includes explicit failed paths while DFS only gets one inference per state. These differences complicate interpretation of relative success rates.

The paper reports single-number results on 1000-example test sets without uncertainty estimates or seed variation. Given stochastic proof selection, random focusing choices, and model training variability, the empirical validity of small reported gaps (e.g., 0.3%) is unclear.

The claim that the model has learned backtracking is only weakly supported: producing syntactically well-formed backtrack instructions that reference existing states does not demonstrate semantically effective backtracking beyond what is already reflected in end-task success.
